candidates.original_title: Eighteen- and 24-month-old infants correct others in anticipation of action mistakes
candidates.description: 24-month-old children's anticipatory helping behavior is influenced by an experimenter's knowledge state about an object's location
candidates.citation_sentence: These results replicate Knudsen and Liszkowski's (2012) findings with 24-month-old children and partially extend them to 3-year-old children.

candidates.original_title: Eighteen-and 24-month-old infants correct others in anticipation of action mistakes
candidates.description: Children inform an experimenter about an object's new location more frequently when the experimenter was absent and therefore ignorant during the object's relocation than when she observed the relocation.
candidates.citation_sentence: Knudsen and Liszkowski (2012) assessed 24-month-old children’s sensitivity to others’ knowledge or ignorance in an anticipatory helping task.
candidates.notes: The 24-month-old group replicated the original finding; the same experiment also tested and partially extended the effect to 3-year-old children.

candidates.original_title: Eighteen-month-old infants show false belief understanding in an active helping paradigm
candidates.description: Infants help an experimenter with a false belief by opening the box containing the desired toy rather than the empty box the experimenter attempts to open.
candidates.citation_sentence: Our interactive task was based closely on a study by Buttelmann et al. (2009).
candidates.notes: The replication omitted the original true-belief comparison condition, which limits interpretation of the result but does not obscure the behavioral replication. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.description: Infants look longer when an experimenter reaches for an object in its actual location rather than the location where she falsely believes it to be.
candidates.citation_sentence: Our initial VOE task was based on the ‘FB-green’ condition from Onishi and Baillargeon’s study (2005).
candidates.notes: Task 2 used a modified version of the original paradigm and found no significant difference in looking time between expected and unexpected reaches. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]

candidates.description: Infants look longer when an experimenter reaches for an object in its actual location rather than the location where she falsely believes it to be.
candidates.citation_sentence: The VOE procedures in Tasks 2 and 3 failed to reproduce evidence that 18-month-old infants’ expectations are violated when an experimenter who ought to have a false belief reaches for an object in its true location (e.g. Onishi & Baillargeon, 2005; Song et al., 2008; Träuble et al., 2010).
candidates.notes: Task 3 was a revised, higher-powered VOE experiment based on Task 2 and the Onishi and Baillargeon paradigm; it again found no significant difference in looking time. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]
